title: Learning to Approximate Uniform Facility Location via Graph Neural Networks
claim: Local neighborhood message passing yields a radius estimate, then open probabilities, and the whole chain trains end-to-end via an unsupervised loss.
layout: 3 stages left-to-right, with a feedback loop arrow underneath labeled gradient loss
description: A horizontal three-stage flow on a white background. At left, a rounded blue-tinted blob holds a small graph of circular nodes. A focal node x is ringed by concentric dashed red circles labeled a1, a2, a3, and purple squiggly arrows show messages flowing into x. The caption reads 'Local message passing including x itself'. A curved black arrow leads to the middle stage, a formula for the radius estimate r-hat as a sum over bins of min{Δ, 1 − t}, with a_i = iΔ and Δ = 1/k, labeled 'Pooling bin contributions'. Another curved arrow leads to the right stage, p_x = min{1, c log(n) r-hat}, labeled 'Computation of open probabilities'. A long rounded return arrow below, labeled '∇ unsupervised loss', runs from the right stage back to the left stage. The eye goes first to the graph, then follows the arrows rightward.
caption: Overview of how MPNN probably recovers a near-optimal solution for the UniFL problem. Local message-passing around a given point $x$ is used to compute an estimate of the radius $r_x$, followed by the computation of the opening probabilities, and MPNN's parameters are computed based on an unsupervised loss via the expected cost of the solution.
abstract: Neural networks, particularly message-passing neural networks (MPNNs), are increasingly used as heuristics for hard combinatorial optimization problems. Yet many learning-based methods rely on supervision, reinforcement learning, or gradient estimators, causing high computational cost, unstable training, or limited guarantees. Classical approximation algorithms provide worst-case guarantees but are non-differentiable and cannot adapt to structure in natural input distributions. We study this tradeoff through Uniform Facility Location (UniFL), a problem with applications in clustering, summarization, logistics, and supply chains. We propose a fully differentiable MPNN that incorporates approximation-algorithmic principles without solver supervision or discrete relaxations. The model has provable approximation guarantees and empirically improves on standard approximation algorithms, narrowing the gap to integer linear programming.
